shorts.title: He Could Have Bought Google for $750K 😳
shorts.description: In 1999, Google was for sale for less than a million dollars. The CEO of Excite said no. This is the most expensive 'no' in internet history.
sources: Wikipedia: Excite (web portal) — 1999 offer to buy Google
Vinod Khosla interviews about the Excite–Google deal

scenes.text: This man could have bought Google… and he said no.
In 1999, Larry Page and Sergey Brin wanted to sell Google and go back to Stanford.
They offered it to George Bell, the CEO of Excite, one of the biggest search engines back then.
The price? Seven hundred and fifty thousand dollars.
Bell thought it was too expensive. He turned it down.
Today, Google is worth over two trillion dollars.
And Excite? Almost nobody remembers it. Would you have bought it?

shorts.title: Blockbuster Could Have Bought Netflix for $50M
shorts.description: In 2000, Netflix offered itself to Blockbuster for $50 million. Blockbuster passed. Ten years later, Blockbuster was bankrupt.

scenes.text: In the year 2000, Netflix was losing money, and its founders flew to Dallas with an offer.
They offered Netflix to Blockbuster, the king of video rentals, for fifty million dollars.
According to co-founder Marc Randolph, Blockbuster's executives could barely keep a straight face.
They said no.
Ten years later, Blockbuster filed for bankruptcy.
Netflix is now worth hundreds of billions. And only one Blockbuster store is left, in Oregon.

shorts.title: He Sold 10% of Apple for $800
shorts.description: Apple had three founders. The third one, Ronald Wayne, sold his 10% stake just 12 days after signing.

scenes.text: Apple wasn't founded by two people. It was founded by three.
In 1976, Steve Jobs, Steve Wozniak and Ronald Wayne started Apple. Wayne got ten percent.
But he was scared of the company's debts.
So just twelve days later, he sold his share for eight hundred dollars.
That ten percent would be worth billions today.
Wayne says he has no regrets. Do you believe him?

shorts.title: He Paid 10,000 Bitcoin for 2 Pizzas 🍕
shorts.description: On May 22, 2010, Laszlo Hanyecz bought two pizzas with 10,000 bitcoin. At bitcoin's peak, that was over a billion dollars.
sources: BitcoinTalk forum post by Laszlo Hanyecz, May 2010

scenes.text: These are the most expensive pizzas in history.
On May twenty second, 2010, a programmer named Laszlo Hanyecz wanted to see if bitcoin could actually buy something.
He offered ten thousand bitcoin to anyone who would bring him two pizzas. Someone said yes.
Back then, that was about forty dollars.
At bitcoin's peak, those coins were worth more than one billion dollars.
Today, May twenty second is Bitcoin Pizza Day. Would you have eaten them?

shorts.title: Kodak Invented the Digital Camera… and It Killed Them
shorts.description: In 1975, a Kodak engineer built the first digital camera. Kodak didn't go all in. In 2012, it filed for bankruptcy.

scenes.text: Kodak invented the digital camera. And that's what destroyed it.
In 1975, a Kodak engineer named Steve Sasson built the very first digital camera.
But Kodak was making a fortune selling film.
Digital cameras threatened that business, so Kodak never fully bet on them.
Other companies did.
In 2012, Kodak filed for bankruptcy.
Sometimes a company's biggest enemy is its own success.

shorts.title: Nokia Had It All… and Lost It in 6 Years
shorts.description: In 2007, Nokia sold almost half of the world's phones. Then the iPhone arrived.
sources: Microsoft press release, Sept 2013: acquisition of Nokia Devices & Services

scenes.text: In 2007, almost half of all phones sold in the world were Nokias.
They were indestructible. Everyone had one.
That same year, the iPhone came out. A touchscreen with no keys? Many thought it was a fad.
They were wrong.
In 2013, Nokia sold its phone business to Microsoft for about five point four billion euros, a fraction of its old value.
Did you have a Nokia?

shorts.title: Lamborghini Exists Because Ferrari Insulted Him 🐂
shorts.description: A tractor maker complained to Enzo Ferrari. The answer he got made him start his own supercar brand.
sources: Ferruccio Lamborghini interviews (story as he told it)

scenes.text: Lamborghini exists because Enzo Ferrari insulted a tractor maker.
Ferruccio Lamborghini got rich building tractors, and he owned several Ferraris.
As the story goes, he complained to Enzo Ferrari about a clutch problem.
And Ferrari basically told him: stick to your tractors.
Lamborghini took it personally. In 1963, he started his own supercar company to beat Ferrari.
Never underestimate an angry man with money.

shorts.title: The Founder of Zara Started as a Delivery Boy
shorts.description: Amancio Ortega left school at 14. Today his company, Inditex, sells clothes almost everywhere on Earth.
sources: Wikipedia: Zara — first store in A Coruña, 1975

scenes.text: One of the richest men in the world started out delivering shirts.
Amancio Ortega left school at fourteen and went to work at a shirt shop in Spain.
Later, with his family, he started making bathrobes.
In 1975, he opened a small store in A Coruña. He called it Zara.
His idea was simple: copy trends fast and have new clothes in stores every few weeks.
Today his company, Inditex, is one of the biggest fashion empires on the planet.

shorts.title: He Started KFC at 62 🍗
shorts.description: Colonel Sanders spent his life switching jobs. At 62, he started franchising his chicken recipe.

scenes.text: If you think it's too late to start, listen to this.
Harland Sanders spent his life switching jobs. Railroad worker, salesman, gas station operator.
In 1952, at sixty two, he started selling his fried chicken recipe to other restaurants.
A few years later, a new highway took the traffic away from his own restaurant.
So he went all in, driving from restaurant to restaurant to sell his recipe. He heard no, again and again.
Today, KFC is in more than one hundred forty countries.
It's never too late.

shorts.title: Nintendo Started in 1889 Selling Playing Cards 🃏
shorts.description: Before Mario, Nintendo sold playing cards and even tried running a taxi company.

scenes.text: Nintendo is older than you think. Much older.
It was founded in 1889, in Kyoto, Japan.
But it didn't make video games. It made playing cards called hanafuda.
In the sixties, it tried anything to survive. A taxi company. Even instant rice.
Almost all of it failed.
Then it bet on toys, and later on video games. Today it's one of the biggest names in entertainment.

shorts.title: Samsung Started Out Selling Dried Fish 🐟
shorts.description: Samsung was founded in 1938 as a small trading company in Daegu, Korea.
sources: Wikipedia: Samsung — founded 1938 by Lee Byung-chul

scenes.text: Your Samsung phone comes from a shop that sold dried fish.
In 1938, Lee Byung-chul founded Samsung in Daegu, Korea.
It was a tiny trading company selling dried fish, vegetables and noodles.
Then it moved into sugar, textiles, insurance…
And at the end of the sixties, it got into electronics.
Today, Samsung is one of the biggest makers of phones and chips on Earth. Is there a Samsung near you right now?

shorts.title: Facebook Rejected Him… Then Paid $19 Billion for His App
shorts.description: In 2009, Facebook didn't hire Brian Acton. Five years later, it bought WhatsApp for $19 billion.
sources: Wikipedia: WhatsApp — acquired by Facebook in 2014

scenes.text: In 2009, Facebook turned this man down for a job.
His name was Brian Acton. He tweeted that it was a great opportunity, and he was moving on.
That same year, he joined his friend Jan Koum on a small messaging app called WhatsApp.
Five years later, Facebook bought it for nineteen billion dollars.
The most expensive rejection in history.

shorts.title: Yahoo Said No to $44.6 Billion
shorts.description: In 2008, Microsoft offered $44.6 billion for Yahoo. Nine years later, Yahoo's core business sold for about a tenth of that.
sources: Wikipedia: Microsoft's proposed acquisition of Yahoo! (2008)

scenes.text: In 2008, Microsoft tried to buy Yahoo for forty four point six billion dollars.
Yahoo said no. They believed they were worth more.
Nine years later, Yahoo sold its core business to Verizon…
for about four and a half billion.
Roughly ten times less.
Sometimes the best offer is the one in front of you.

shorts.title: 13 Employees. $1 Billion. Instagram
shorts.description: In 2012, Facebook bought Instagram for $1 billion. It had 13 employees and almost no revenue.
sources: Wikipedia: Instagram — acquired by Facebook, April 2012

scenes.text: In 2012, a company with just thirteen employees sold for one billion dollars.
It was Instagram. It was less than two years old and had barely made any money.
Mark Zuckerberg bought it anyway.
People called it insane.
Today Instagram has over two billion users and makes billions every year.
It wasn't insane. It was one of the best deals ever made.

shorts.title: Play-Doh Was Originally a Wallpaper Cleaner 🤯
shorts.description: A cleaning product about to disappear became one of the most famous toys ever.
sources: Wikipedia: Play-Doh — Kutol Products, Kay Zufall

scenes.text: The modeling clay you played with as a kid was a cleaning product.
In the 1930s, a company called Kutol sold a putty to clean soot off wallpaper.
But home heating changed, people stopped buying it, and the company was about to go under.
Then a teacher noticed kids could use it to make shapes.
They removed the detergent, added colors, and Play-Doh was born.
Billions of cans have been sold since.
